article.title: Why UX Research Before Development Saves Rework
article.description: See how interviews, journey maps, prototypes, and usability tests can clarify product decisions before development begins.
article.intro: Teams often move directly from an idea to a screen. A small amount of research first can reveal the real task, the language users understand, and the assumptions most likely to cause rework.

sections.heading: Understand the user’s context
paragraphs: Talk with people who will actually use the product. Ask about their current process, goals, workarounds, and the moments where they lose time or confidence.
Combine those conversations with support requests and product data where available. The aim is to find patterns, not to treat one opinion as a complete answer.

sections.heading: Prototype the critical journey
paragraphs: Map the steps from a user’s starting point to a successful outcome. Sketch or prototype the route before investing in polished design and engineering.
Test whether people can complete the task without coaching. Watch where they hesitate, then adjust labels, structure, or flow before building the full experience.

sections.heading: Carry learning into development
paragraphs: Document the user need behind important design choices. This helps engineers and stakeholders make consistent decisions when details change during implementation.
Research should continue after launch. Feedback and observed behavior can reveal new needs and show whether the product is delivering the intended value.

sections.heading: Turn findings into clear product decisions
paragraphs: A research report is only valuable if it changes what the team builds. Summarize the main user needs, supporting evidence, open questions, and recommended next actions. Distinguish what was observed from what the team inferred.

Prioritize issues by how strongly they affect a core task. A confusing step in sign-up may deserve attention before a visual preference that few people notice. Bring design, engineering, and business stakeholders into the review.

Keep a lightweight record of decisions so future work can build on what was learned. When new evidence challenges an earlier assumption, update the plan openly rather than defending a design because it has already been made.

takeaways: Research the task, not only visual preferences.
Test a prototype before full development.
